query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount (~0.5 at%) of interstitial carbon into a single‐phase FCC CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of nanoscale carbide precipitates that pin grain boundaries, refine the microstructure, and thereby improve mechanical durability, reduce room‐temperature creep strain under sustained loads, and enhance corrosion resistance compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed single‐phase FCC CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy produced via powder metallurgy without any interstitial additions.
generation.intervention: Add a trace amount (~0.5 at%) of carbon during alloying to enable interstitial alloying and in situ carbide precipitation during consolidation and controlled cooling.
generation.conditions: Room‐temperature service as experienced by aerospace fasteners under sustained mechanical loads and exposure to saline or chlorine‐rich environments (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl).
generation.structural_mediator: The interstitial carbon facilitates the nucleation of uniformly dispersed, fine carbide particles along grain boundaries and within the matrix, which act as pinning sites that stabilize grain boundaries and promote a refined, homogeneous microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Carbon atoms provide additional solid solution strengthening and trigger the in situ formation of nanoscale carbides during processing. These carbides reduce local strain concentrations by pinning grain boundaries and hindering dislocation motion under constant load (thus improving room‐temperature creep resistance) while simultaneously reducing active sites for corrosive attack, leading to a more robust passivation film and enhanced corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated CoCrFeMnNi HEA, the carbon‐modified alloy is expected to show a higher yield strength and mechanical durability, a decreased room‐temperature creep strain rate under sustained load, and a lower corrosion current density in saline media.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the standard CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy fabricated without any intentional interstitial carbon addition, which exhibits moderate mechanical properties, undefined room‐temperature creep behavior under long-term loading, and standard corrosion performance in saline solutions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated for low carbon contents (approximately 0.3–0.7 at%); exceeding this range may result in excessive carbide precipitation leading to embrittlement. The improvements are also tied to using processing routes (powder metallurgy with controlled cooling) that enable fine carbide dispersion.
generation.uncertainty: While interstitial carbon has been shown to improve strength and ductility in TWIP‐TRIP HEAs (e.g., PMC5227964::web::011::deformation_mechanisms) and grain-boundary modifications enhance creep resistance at elevated temperatures (PMC9848264::web::003::introduction), the extension of these benefits to room‐temperature creep behavior and integrated corrosion resistance in aerospace fasteners remains to be verified. The interplay of fine carbide precipitation with long-term creep and corrosion under service conditions is not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using identical powder metallurgy routes and cooling profiles: (a) a control group of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA without carbon addition and (b) a test group with ~0.5 at% carbon added. Characterize the microstructures using TEM, SEM-EDS, and XRD to confirm the formation and distribution of carbide precipitates. Subject both groups to constant tensile loading at room temperature for extended durations to measure creep strain rates, and perform potentiodynamic polarization tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution to assess corrosion parameters.
measurements: Yield strength and ductility from standard tensile tests
Room-temperature creep strain rate under constant load over time
Corrosion current density, corrosion potential, and passivation behavior from electrochemical tests
Microstructural observations of carbide distribution and grain boundary characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-added alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in room-temperature creep strain rate and improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., lower corrosion current and higher passivation potential) relative to the control, or if the microstructure reveals coarsened or deleterious carbide precipitates that induce embrittlement, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHighly entropy alloys (HEAs) are novel materials that have great potential for application in aerospace and marine engineering due to their superior mechanical properties and benefits over conventional materials. NiCrCoFe, also referred to as Ni-based HEA, has exceptional low-temperature strength and microstructural stability. However, HEAs have limited corrosion resistance in some environments, such as a 3.5 wt% sodium chloride (NaCl) solution. Adding corrosion-resistant elements such as molybdenum (Mo) to HEAs is expected to increase their corrosion resistance in a variety of corrosive environments. Metal additive manufacturing reduces production times compared to casting and eliminates shrinkage issues, making it ideal for producing homogeneous HEA. This study used directed energy deposition (DED) to create Cr25-xCo25Ni25Fe25Mox (x = 0, 5, 10%) HEAs. Tensile strength and potentiodynamic polarization tests were used to assess the materials’ mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEAs unify all known metallurgical strengthening effects in one single bulk material: i) massive substitutional solid solution strengthening due to multiple principle elements (i.e., Fe, Mn, Co and Cr); ii) interstitial solid solution strengthening by carbon; iii) micro-composite effect from dual-phase structure; iv) nano-particle strengthening from nano-carbides (Figs 2b and 4c); v) nano-twinning induced plasticity effect (TWIP) (Fig. 4b); vi) displacive transformation induced plasticity effect (TRIP) (Fig. 4a); vii) formation of stacking faults (Fig. 4b); viii) grain size reduction (increased grain boundary density); and dislocation hardening (Fig. 4b).

AbstractStrong and ductile materials that have high resistance to corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement are rare and yet essential for realizing safety-critical energy infrastructures, hydrogen-based industries, and transportation solutions. Here we report how we reconcile these constraints in the form of a strong and ductile CoNiV medium-entropy alloy with face-centered cubic structure. It shows high resistance to hydrogen embrittlement at ambient temperature at a strain rate of 10−4 s−1, due to its low hydrogen diffusivity and the deformation twinning that impedes crack propagation. Moreover, a dense oxide film formed on the alloy’s surface reduces the hydrogen uptake rate, and provides high corrosion resistance in dilute sulfuric acid with a corrosion current density below 7 μA cm−2.
